# Stationary calibration and Adam {#sec-stationary-calibration}

## Frozen kernels and probability laws

For the driver family of @sec-general-framework, let $H:\Theta\times\mathsf X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a measurable innovation and write $H_\theta(x)=H(\theta,x)$. The stationary EMA construction uses only the following frozen assumptions on the standard Borel driver space.

::: {#asm-frozen-driver}
## Frozen driver and innovation moment

For each $\theta\in\Theta$, $P_\theta$ has a unique invariant probability $\pi_\theta$, and

$$
\pi_\theta(\|H_\theta\|^2)<\infty.
$$
:::

All subsequent stationary constructions are pointwise in $\theta$; no regularity of the family of invariant laws is assumed here. Under @asm-frozen-driver, the consistent stationary finite-dimensional laws specified by $\pi_\theta$ and $P_\theta$ extend, by the Kolmogorov extension theorem, to a two-sided stationary Markov chain $(X_k^\theta)_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ on this standard Borel space. Denote its law on $(\mathsf{X}^{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal A^{\otimes\mathbb{Z}})$ by $\mathbb{P}_\theta^{\mathrm{stat}}$. Its one-time marginal is $\pi_\theta$, and its forward transition conditional on the entire past is $P_\theta$. The marginal $\pi_\theta$ describes one observation; $\mathbb{P}_\theta^{\mathrm{stat}}$ also describes temporal dependence and is generally not a product law.

The ordinary frozen mean field is

$$
h(\theta)=\pi_\theta(H_\theta)
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_\theta^{\mathrm{stat}}}[H_\theta(X_0^\theta)].
$$ {#eq-ordinary-frozen-field}

A Robbins--Monro root $\theta^\star$ satisfies $h(\theta^\star)=0$. For acceptance-rate calibration one may use $H_\theta(x)=a_\theta(x)-a^\star$, where $a_\theta(x)$ is the conditional expected acceptance probability and $a^\star$ is the target rate. If the observed residual instead uses proposals or acceptance indicators, the driving state must include the variables needed to make that observation a function of its current state; the invariant law in @eq-ordinary-frozen-field then refers to that enlarged driver.

## Fixed-gain memories and the stationary field

For context, a controlled recursion generates observations according to

$$
X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n\sim P_{\theta_n}(X_n,\cdot),
$$ {#eq-controlled-transition}

with $\theta_n,X_n$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_n$. Ordinary Robbins--Monro adaptation takes the form

$$
\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+\gamma_{n+1}H_{\theta_n}(X_{n+1}).
$$ {#eq-rm-update}

Here $(\gamma_n)$ are positive deterministic parameter gains. An Adam-type alternative fixes $0\leq\alpha,\beta<1$ and $\varepsilon>0$ and uses

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_{n+1}&=\alpha M_n+(1-\alpha)H_{\theta_n}(X_{n+1}),\\
V_{n+1}&=\beta V_n+(1-\beta)H_{\theta_n}(X_{n+1})^{\odot2},\\
\theta_{n+1}&=\theta_n+\gamma_{n+1}
\frac{M_{n+1}}{\sqrt{V_{n+1}}+\varepsilon}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-adam-recursion}

Initially $M_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $V_0\in[0,\infty)^d$. Squares, square roots and division are componentwise, and $\varepsilon$ is added in each coordinate. We use uncorrected memories, without finite-time bias factors. The gains $1-\alpha$ and $1-\beta$ remain fixed. This is @eq-general-memory-recursion with memory $U_n=(M_n,V_n)$ and readout $G(x,m,v)=m/(\sqrt v+\varepsilon)$.

Fix $\theta$ and set $Y_k^\theta=H_\theta(X_k^\theta)$. Define the stationary memories at time zero by

$$
M^\theta=(1-\alpha)\sum_{j=0}^\infty\alpha^j Y_{-j}^\theta,\qquad
V^\theta=(1-\beta)\sum_{j=0}^\infty\beta^j(Y_{-j}^\theta)^{\odot2}.
$$ {#eq-stationary-memories}

For a zero coefficient the corresponding series consists only of its $j=0$ term. These variables are defined under $\mathbb{P}_\theta^{\mathrm{stat}}$.

::: {#lem-stationary-memories}
## Integrable stationary memories

Under @asm-frozen-driver, the series in @eq-stationary-memories converge absolutely almost surely and in $L^1$. Moreover, $M^\theta\in L^2$.
:::

The proof is given in [Appendix A](#sec-stationary-series-proof).

The stationary Adam field is

$$
F(\theta)
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_\theta^{\mathrm{stat}}}
\left[\frac{M^\theta}{\sqrt{V^\theta}+\varepsilon}\right].
$$ {#eq-adam-field}

It is finite because $\|M^\theta/(\sqrt{V^\theta}+\varepsilon)\|\leq\|M^\theta\|/\varepsilon$. This expectation is under the stationary frozen Markov path law, not the nonstationary law of @eq-controlled-transition--@eq-adam-recursion. For the IID kernel $P_\theta(x,\cdot)=\pi_\theta(\cdot)$ it reduces to the history field of [@Dereich2025_UJMNX8NK, Definition 1.3]. Neither the field's existence nor the memory construction requires the additional restriction $\alpha^2<\beta$ used in their ODE theorem.

## Adam as a Markov augmentation

Fix $\theta$. Let $\mathsf Y=\mathbb{R}^d\times[0,\infty)^d$ be the memory space, with its Euclidean product norm, and let $\mathsf Z=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$ carry the product sigma-algebra. Define

$$
T_\theta(x',m,v)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha m+(1-\alpha)H_\theta(x')\\
\beta v+(1-\beta)H_\theta(x')^{\odot2}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-memory-map}

For $u=(m,v)$, also write $T_\theta(x,u)=T_\theta(x,m,v)$. For the frozen recursions, $Z_n=(X_n,M_n,V_n)$ therefore has the kernel $Q_\theta$ in @eq-augmented-kernel.

For two memory states driven by the same observation,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|T_\theta(x',m,v)-T_\theta(x',\widetilde m,\widetilde v)\|^2
&=\alpha^2\|m-\widetilde m\|^2+\beta^2\|v-\widetilde v\|^2\\
&\leq\kappa^2\|(m,v)-(\widetilde m,\widetilde v)\|^2,
\qquad \kappa=\max\{\alpha,\beta\}<1.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-same-driver-memory-contraction}

Thus the memory difference contracts along a common driving path, with coefficient $\kappa=\max\{\alpha,\beta\}$. This estimate suffices to identify the invariant memory law under @asm-frozen-driver.

## Identification of the stationary memories

::: {#cor-stationary-memory-law}
## Stationary memory representation

Under @asm-frozen-driver, $Q_\theta$ has a unique invariant probability $\nu_\theta$. Its driving marginal is $\pi_\theta$ and

$$
\nu_\theta=
\operatorname{Law}_{\mathbb{P}_\theta^{\mathrm{stat}}}
(X_0^\theta,M^\theta,V^\theta),
$$ {#eq-stationary-joint-law}

where $M^\theta,V^\theta$ are the stationary histories in @eq-stationary-memories. Consequently,

$$
F(\theta)=\int_{\mathsf Z}
\frac{m}{\sqrt v+\varepsilon}\,
\nu_\theta(dx\,dm\,dv).
$$ {#eq-stationary-adam-integral}
:::

::: {.proof}
Define $M_k^\theta$ and $V_k^\theta$ by shifting the infinite series in @eq-stationary-memories to time $k$. Their almost-sure convergence follows from @lem-stationary-memories and stationarity. They satisfy the frozen recursions, while the joint process $(X_k^\theta,M_k^\theta,V_k^\theta)_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ is stationary. Its one-time law is therefore invariant for @eq-augmented-kernel.

For uniqueness, let $\eta$ be another invariant probability of $Q_\theta$. By the marginal identity in @sec-general-framework and @asm-frozen-driver, its driving marginal equals $\pi_\theta$. Couple initial states with laws $\eta$ and $\nu_\theta$ so that their driving coordinates agree, and then use the same driving transitions for both memory recursions. Their memory difference after $n$ steps is bounded by $\kappa^n\|U_0-\widetilde U_0\|$. This tends to zero almost surely without a moment assumption on the two initial memories. For every bounded measurable test function that is uniformly Lipschitz in the memory coordinate, bounded convergence gives equality of the two stationary expectations. Such tests determine probability measures on $\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, hence $\eta=\nu_\theta$. The integral representation follows from @lem-stationary-memories and $\varepsilon>0$.
:::

The stationary representation follows from the invariant driver law, its innovation moment and synchronous memory contraction. Under the additional hypotheses of @thm-wasserstein-lifting and finite first moments in its metric, the invariant law constructed there is the same $\nu_\theta$. In the affine EMA setting, the synchronous argument above gives uniqueness among all invariant probabilities.

## Calibration under linear and nonlinear memory

Linear EMA momentum preserves the ordinary field. By the absolute integrability just proved, expectation and summation can be interchanged:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_\theta^{\mathrm{stat}}}[M^\theta]
=(1-\alpha)\sum_{j\geq0}\alpha^j\mathbb{E}[Y_{-j}^\theta]
=h(\theta).
$$ {#eq-momentum-preservation}

No independence is used. Adam instead multiplies each momentum coordinate by $W_i^\theta=(\sqrt{V_i^\theta}+\varepsilon)^{-1}$. Since $0<W_i^\theta\leq\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $M_i^\theta\in L^2$, the covariance below is well defined. Expanding its definition gives

$$
F_i(\theta)=h_i(\theta)\,\mathbb{E}[W_i^\theta]
+\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathbb{P}_\theta^{\mathrm{stat}}}(M_i^\theta,W_i^\theta).
$$ {#eq-covariance-decomposition}

Consequently, at an ordinary root,

$$
F_i(\theta^\star)
=\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathbb{P}_{\theta^\star}^{\mathrm{stat}}}
(M_i^{\theta^\star},W_i^{\theta^\star}).
$$ {#eq-covariance-at-root}

Thus an ordinary root is also an Adam root exactly when these componentwise covariances vanish. The identity isolates the calibration issue: centring the innovation centres the first memory, but does not by itself centre the normalised readout. Determining the sign or size of the covariance, and the resulting root displacement, requires analysis of a particular model.

## Verification of the memory and readout hypotheses

For @eq-memory-map, use $d_Y(u,v)=\|u-v\|$ and write

$$
T_\theta(x,u)=Au+b_\theta(x),\quad
A=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha I_d,\beta I_d),\quad
b_\theta(x)=\begin{pmatrix}(1-\alpha)H_\theta(x)\\(1-\beta)H_\theta(x)^{\odot2}\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-affine-memory}

If $b_\theta$ is $L_b$-Lipschitz in $d_X$, then @eq-memory-joint-lipschitz holds with $r=\max\{\alpha,\beta\}$ and $L_T=L_b$. The one-step first-moment condition in @asm-memory-lipschitz can be checked using @lem-augmented-drift when its weight controls the metric. Spatial regularity of $b_\theta$ requires checking the metric and innovation together, in addition to the stationary second-moment assumption.

### Square-root second-moment coordinates

There is a distinction between regularity of the memory update and regularity of its readout. The map $(m,v)\mapsto m/(\sqrt v+\varepsilon)$ is not globally Lipschitz in $v$ under the ordinary Euclidean metric near $v=0$. For a bounded innovation, however, a change of memory coordinates removes this difficulty without modifying the Adam recursion.

Assume, for the remainder of this subsection, that

$$
\|H_\theta(x)\|_\infty\leq B_H,\qquad
\|H_\theta(x)-H_\theta(y)\|\leq L_Hd_X(x,y).
$$ {#eq-bounded-innovation}

Put $S_n=\sqrt{V_n}$ coordinatewise and use the forward-invariant memory set

$$
\mathsf Y_B=\{(m,s):\|m\|_\infty\leq B_H,\quad
0\leq s_i\leq B_H\},
$$

with metric $d_Y((m,s),(m',s'))=\|m-m'\|+\|s-s'\|$. With initial memories $(M_0,S_0)\in\mathsf Y_B$, the update is

$$
\widehat T_\theta(x,m,s)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha m+(1-\alpha)H_\theta(x)\\
\sqrt{\beta s^{\odot2}+(1-\beta)H_\theta(x)^{\odot2}}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-sqrt-memory-update}

For each coordinate, the second component is the Euclidean norm of $(\sqrt\beta\,s_i,\sqrt{1-\beta}\,H_{\theta,i}(x))$. The reverse triangle inequality therefore gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
d_Y(\widehat T_\theta(x,u),\widehat T_\theta(y,v))
\leq {}&\max\{\alpha,\sqrt\beta\}\,d_Y(u,v)\\
&+\bigl(1-\alpha+\sqrt{1-\beta}\bigr)L_Hd_X(x,y).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-sqrt-memory-contraction}

Thus the transformed memory satisfies @eq-memory-joint-lipschitz, with contraction coefficient $\max\{\alpha,\sqrt\beta\}<1$. On $\mathsf Y_B$ the Adam readout

$$
G(m,s)=\frac{m}{s+\varepsilon}
$$ {#eq-adam-lipschitz-readout}

is Lipschitz:

$$
\|G(m,s)-G(m',s')\|
\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\|m-m'\|
+B_H\varepsilon^{-2}\|s-s'\|.
$$ {#eq-adam-readout-lipschitz}

These coordinates represent the same finite-dimensional memory process. Since the transformed memory is bounded, a driver one-step first moment supplies the remaining moment condition in @asm-memory-lipschitz. It gives a direct Lipschitz observable for the Poisson equation when the innovation is bounded, as for an acceptance-rate residual. For unbounded innovations the affine $(m,v)$ representation still admits @thm-wasserstein-lifting under its stated assumptions; the Lipschitz property of the Adam readout must then be addressed separately.
